meta.engine: PostgreSQL 17.4 (local) + pgvector 0.8.0 HNSW (compiled from source with MSVC 19.43, Windows PostgreSQL build)
meta.pg_version: PostgreSQL 17.4 on x86_64-windows, compiled by msvc-19.42.34436, 64-bit

protocol.distance_operators: search uses <-> (L2), matching the vector_l2_ops index opclass; note the cosine operator <=> was used in the first (discarded) run and silently forced a Seq Scan -- see resolution_of_plan_check
protocol.episode: search1 -> engine structural rewrite (REINDEX and/or CLUSTER) -> search2; table content unchanged, so any top-10 difference is an index-generation tear (A4)

resolution_of_plan_check.symptom: first U1 run: plan_uses_hnsw=False but recall_vs_exact=0.584 (not ~1.0) -- mutually exclusive if the query had really been a seq scan
resolution_of_plan_check.root_cause: the search SQL used the COSINE operator <=> while the index was built with the L2 opclass vector_l2_ops; pgvector does NOT reject the mismatch, the planner silently falls back to Seq Scan + Sort by cosine distance, whose ranking differs from the L2 ranking the recall reference uses -> apparent recall = 0.584

discriminating_evidence.plan_literal_l2: Index Scan using u1_vectors_embedding_hnsw (after the fix to <->): HNSW path confirmed
discriminating_evidence.plan_literal_cosine: Limit -> Sort -> Seq Scan on u1_vectors (opclass/operator mismatch, no index)
discriminating_evidence.ef_search_sensitivity: with <=> the same top-10 came back for ef_search in {10,40,64,1000} (no index involved); the plan probe was right, the old queries never touched the graph
discriminating_evidence.distance_scale_check: PG <=> returned ~0.12 for L2 true distances ~5.6: cosine distance on all-positive vectors, confirming the metric mismatch
discriminating_evidence.recall_after_fix: literal-form recall@10 recomputed with <-> rises from 0.584 to the values recorded in the rerun cells

resolution_of_plan_check.action_taken: all search SQL switched to <-> (L2); the old U1 numbers were discarded and U1 rerun; each cell records plan_sample_explain and hnsw_path_forced_with_enable_seqscan_off

api_quirks: pgvector requires ef_construction >= 2*m: the paper's FAISS-style (m=32, ef_construction=40) is rejected with InvalidParameterValue. Used ef_construction=64 (the minimum allowed for m=32).

Operator/opclass mismatch is SILENT: searching with the cosine operator '<=>' against a vector_l2_ops HNSW index raises no error; the planner quietly falls back to Seq Scan + Sort by cosine distance (the first U1 run was built on this mistake -- see resolution_of_plan_check).
'REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY' cannot run inside a transaction block (captured verbatim in the P cell probe).
Plain REINDEX takes an AccessExclusiveLock on table+index: with an open reader transaction it blocks until lock_timeout fires (P cell probe b, 3.0 s) -- the structural rewrite path quiesces readers.

A client-driven 20 000-row UPDATE (execute_values, page_size=1000) was ~100x slower than the equivalent single server-side UPDATE ... FROM (SELECT row_number() OVER (ORDER BY random())); the G cell now generates its permutation server-side.
Windows-specific: backend spawn can fail with "could not reserve shared memory region for child (error code 487)"; retry / per-cell runs are needed in this environment (not a pgvector issue).
deviations: Milvus was not deployed in this environment. The recorded native engine controls use PostgreSQL/pgvector; no Milvus measurements are included.
pgvector used a local PostgreSQL 17.4 instance on port 5439 rather than a container. pgvector 0.8.0 was compiled with MSVC 19.43 and loaded from its built library.
Index parameter deviation: ef_construction=64 (pgvector's minimum for m=32) instead of the paper's FAISS value 40; m=32, k=10, ef_search=64 and the L2 metric all match the paper's protocol.

FIRST U1 RUN DISCARDED: it searched with the cosine operator '<=>' against the L2 index; pgvector silently seq-scanned, and the L2-based recall reference turned that into an apparent 0.584 'recall'. All searches now use '<->' (L2); U1 was rerun. Evidence and reasoning: meta.resolution_of_plan_check.

The D cell's first run reported recall_vs_surviving_exact=0.0, which was our bug: the numpy reference returned positions inside the compressed surviving array instead of original row ids. Fixed (np.flatnonzero maps back) and D was rerun; final values 0.9385 / 0.944.

Cell G implements 'same vectors, different insertion order' with the engine's own CLUSTER (heap rewrite by a server-side random permutation + HNSW rebuild); the permutation is generated by the server (row_number() OVER (ORDER BY random())) rather than by numpy's rng, and the client-driven UPDATE was replaced by one server-side statement (see api_quirks).
Scale/seed: one seed (20261008), N=20000, 200 queries per cell (200 episodes/cell). Seed 20261009 is not included in this record.
Milvus-style multi-segment 'compaction' has no direct analogue in pgvector: its structural rewrite is REINDEX (and CLUSTER), so 'compaction' here means the engine's own index-rebuild path.

ENVIRONMENT: the Windows PostgreSQL server log records "could not reserve shared memory region for child ... error code 487" (ERROR_INVALID_ADDRESS, a known Windows/ASLR issue) plus several "could not send data to client / connection to client lost" events; these abort a backend spawn or the client connection and are the cause of the three aborted U2 attempts before the runs were split per cell. No effect on the recorded cells: every cell completed and reported its own row counts, plans and timings.
limitations: pgvector does not expose the HNSW adjacency of a built index; structural tear (A5) NOT measurable in-engine; answer level (A4) only.

Milvus (first-choice engine) unreachable in this sandbox: Docker daemon could not start (see report); pgvector fallback executed on a local PostgreSQL 17.4 instance instead of the planned docker pgvector:pg16 image.

unpinned_reindex_tear.note: same heap order, rebuilt by the engine: ~4.5-7% of episodes differ by <=2 of 10 ids; serial and parallel rebuilds show the same magnitude -> the small tear is rebuild non-determinism, not an order/generation effect

insertion_order_generation_change.note: a real generation change (heap/insertion order) tears 89.5% of episodes (mean 4.27 of 10 ids); repeating the search on one generation is 0% -> the tear is the generation change

pinned.note: with the rewrite inside an open REPEATABLE READ transaction tear is 0.000 (the engine defers the swap until the pinned reader commits); the same rewrite seen post-commit shows 0.070

deletion_path.note: no ghost ids ever surface (MVCC filters deletes); recall held; REINDEX reclaims the dead tuples' index space

DET_s20261008.question: is a bulk HNSW rebuild a pure function of heap order? compare two consecutive REINDEXes under the default parallel maintenance workers and under a serial build

G_s20261008.index_construction: bulk CREATE INDEX on the heap in id order; then CLUSTER USING <perm btree> (rewrites the heap in a random permutation and rebuilds every index, incl. HNSW) -> REINDEX
G_s20261008.generation_change: generation A = HNSW over heap in id order; generation B = HNSW bulk-rebuilt over heap in random-permutation order (the pgvector analogue of the paper's FAISS 'same vectors, different insertion order' protocol)
